hints.title: Write the counterexample test
hints.body: A counterexample to an IF–THEN claim makes the IF part true and the THEN part false. Check the product-divisibility condition before considering the conclusion.
hints.recap: A failed premise cannot disprove an implication.
hints.pitfall: A number being a factor means exact integer division, not merely being smaller.
hints.pause: For each row, calculate the product and check whether the proposed divisor divides it.

recall.reminder: A failed premise cannot disprove an implication.

hints.title: Negate the whole OR conclusion
hints.body: The conclusion is an inclusive OR. To make it false, both of its alternatives must fail. Record the two individual divisibility tests alongside the product test.
hints.recap: An OR statement fails only when neither alternative holds.
hints.pitfall: One failed alternative is not enough if the other alternative is true.
hints.pause: Complete the three tests for every row and select precisely the rows with a true premise and false conclusion.

recall.reminder: An OR statement fails only when neither alternative holds.

solution:
1. Identify the required logical pattern. We need a to divide bc, but to divide neither b nor c.

2. Test the three rows. In I, bc=200 and 5 divides it, but 5 also divides 10 and 20, so the conclusion is true. In II, bc=16 and 8 divides 16, while 8 divides neither 4 nor 4, so the conclusion is false. In III, bc=84 and 6 divides it; although 6 does not divide 7, it does divide 12, so the OR conclusion is true.

3. Select the counterexample. Only II has a true premise and a false conclusion.

Answer C.
knowledgePattern: Test whether a product-divisibility implication has a true premise and a false disjunction
